name: Mickey Moore

inspiration.oldScript: The silent Shape stalks teenage girls and cuts down the ones who have boyfriends, tie up the phone or laugh too loud, sparing only the virginal babysitter: purity as the price of surviving the night.
inspiration.newLens: The Shape is a 1971 babysitter a town rumor branded a bad girl and sent away for loving another girl. She enforces the purity rules because they broke her, and the crew wins by tearing the rulebook up so that everyone, bad girls included, lives to see November.

logline: Every Halloween a pale, silent shape in a hand-knit cardigan walks Crystal Street, and every babysitter who answers the phone hears the same thing on the line: the click, click, click of knitting needles.
backstory: In 1971 Michaela "Mickey" Moore was the best babysitter on Crystal Street: sixteen, freckled, a shortstop on the girls' softball team, and never without her knitting bag. On Halloween night she sat for baby Teddy Kettering on Crystal Street, and her best friend June Albright came over to watch the Creature Feature. Somewhere in the second movie the girls kissed. Carol Lund, the babysitter next door, saw it through the window. She could not bring herself to say what she saw, so she called the KGLM Party Line the next morning and told the whole valley a story it would believe: that Mickey had snuck a boy in through the back window and, while they were busy on the couch, baby Teddy crawled out the dog door and was found at midnight in the Heartstone roundabout. Mickey was fired, shunned at church, and sent to the Valley Haven School for Girls, where they made her wear a plaster mask of her own face in deportment class to practice a pleasant expression. On Halloween 1972 she ran away to walk home in the fog on Quarry Road. She never arrived. They found only her cardigan, folded on the Crystal Street sign. Every Halloween since, her shape walks home in that mask and that cardigan, and she enforces every rule that broke her: the sitter who answers the phone, the couple on the couch, the girl who laughs too loud.

centralIssue.title: The purity rules that broke her
centralIssue.summary: Mickey was never a bad sitter and never a bad girl. A frightened neighbor turned a first kiss into a scandal, and the town chose the rumor over the truth because the truth scared it more. Her blade is the town's own rulebook. Prove what really happened that night, name who started the lie, and show her a Halloween where nobody has to be pure to survive.

poster: A tall, silent young woman in a long cranberry hand-knit cardigan and a pale blank plaster mask standing motionless in the middle of a leafy suburban cul-de-sac on Halloween night, a pair of long steel knitting needles in one hand, jack-o'-lanterns glowing on every porch, a babysitter's silhouette at a lit kitchen window behind her
portrait: Close portrait of a pale, expressionless plaster mask with faint fingerprints pressed into its cheeks, surrounded by loose auburn curls and the high collar of a cranberry cable-knit cardigan, a strand of yarn trailing from a steel knitting needle raised beside the mask, cold streetlight from one side
endingPhoto: A tall, silent young woman in a long cranberry hand-knit cardigan and a pale blank plaster mask standing motionless behind billowing white laundry on a backyard clothesline on Halloween night, steel knitting needles in one hand, jack-o'-lanterns glowing on the porch steps, teens in costumes freezing at the picket fence
taunts: A good sitter keeps the line clear.
No boys. No phone. No laughing after nine. Rules are rules.
Knit one, purl two. Lights out by ten.
I followed every rule but one. Look where it got me.
Smile, sweetheart. Practice a pleasant expression.

clues.title: The Party Line tape
clues.hint: In 1971 the whole valley heard its gossip on KGLM's morning call-in show, and the station never throws a tape away.

encounter.title: Reel 71-11-01
encounter.text: The KGLM archive is a closet of reel-to-reel tapes stacked to the ceiling, each box labeled in grease pencil. THE PARTY LINE WITH BUD DELACORTE, NOV 1 1971 sits on top of the pile, dust-free, as if someone has been playing it. The station logbook beside it is open to the same date. In the booth down the hall, the call-in line lights up by itself.
encounter.art: A cramped radio station closet stacked to the ceiling with flat reel-to-reel tape boxes marked in grease pencil, one box on top wiped clean of dust while the rest are gray, a thick station logbook lying open beside it, a teenager lifting the clean box down, and through the doorway down the hall a red call-in bulb glowing on an empty booth console, dim bulb and red glow, medium shot

choices.label: Thread the reel on the old deck and listen

success.text: Between a recipe for tuna casserole and a lost beagle, a girl's voice says, "I won't give my name, but I sit for the Hendersons and I saw it with my own eyes." A boy in the window, a baby in the roundabout. In the logbook, Bud wrote the caller down anyway: Carol L., 16, Pinecone Lane.
success.art: A reel-to-reel tape deck spinning under a desk lamp, a teenager in headphones leaning close, an open station logbook with one handwritten line circled in red grease pencil

failure.text: The reel spins too fast and the voices squeal into chipmunk gossip. Then it slows, and slows, until all that comes out of the speaker is a steady click, click, click, like needles. The tape snaps. The call-in light goes dark.
failure.art: A snapped reel of brown audio tape curling off an old tape deck in a dark radio booth, a single red call-in light fading out above the console

choices.label: Answer the lit call-in line on air

success.text: Nobody speaks. Instead the line plays back a tinny recording of the 1971 show, and the caller giggles nervously before she gives her first name by accident: "Carol. I mean, just a concerned neighbor." Somewhere on the line, needles stop clicking, as if someone else was listening too.
success.art: A teenager in an overnight radio booth holding a phone receiver to one ear, eyes wide, the glowing on-air sign lit red, the window behind them showing the water tower against a moonlit sky

failure.text: You say hello to the whole sleeping valley. On the line, a girl whispers, "A good sitter keeps the line clear," and every phone on the switchboard lights up at once. You yank the cord and sit in the dark, shaking.
failure.art: A radio station switchboard with every button lit at once, a yanked phone cord dangling, a frightened teenager in the dim booth lit by the blinking lights

clues.title: Doris Kettering's date book
clues.hint: The family Mickey sat for that Halloween still lives on Crystal Street, and this week they are clearing out the garage.

encounter.title: Everything Must Go
encounter.place: Garage sale, the Kettering house, Crystal Street
encounter.text: Mrs. Doris Kettering has dragged fifteen years of her family onto card tables in the driveway: a bassinet, a fondue set, a box marked TEDDY'S BABY THINGS 1971. She keeps glancing at the box and away from it. Her son Teddy, sixteen now and mortified, is pricing records. Every one of her porch lights is on in broad daylight.
encounter.art: A sunny suburban driveway garage sale, folding tables of 1970s household goods, a bassinet, a fondue set and a cardboard box of baby clothes, a nervous middle-aged woman in a pastel pantsuit glancing at the box and away, her sixteen-year-old son pricing a crate of records, every porch light on the house switched on in broad daylight, a teenager holding two quarters out to her, bright afternoon sun, wide shot

choices.label: Haggle for the whole baby box, sight unseen

success.text: Two quarters and a promise to take the bassinet too. Under the bibs is Doris's 1971 date book. October 31: Home 11:40. Teddy asleep in his crib. Girls asleep on the couch, holding hands. Dishes done! Then November 2, in smaller writing: I know Carol's story is a lie. Hal says it's better this way.
success.art: A teenager kneeling on a driveway beside an open cardboard box of baby clothes, reading a small 1971 date book, one handwritten entry underlined, a bassinet beside them

failure.text: Doris snatches the box back. "That one isn't for sale. I don't know how it got out here." She carries it inside and locks the door. That night, the box sits on her front step again, and the bassinet is rocking by itself.
failure.art: A cardboard baby box on a suburban front step at night, an empty white bassinet rocking beside it under a glowing porch light

choices.label: Ask Mrs. Kettering who used to babysit Teddy

success.text: Her hands stop on the fondue forks. "Mickey Moore. She was wonderful. She even did the dishes." Then it pours out: Teddy was asleep in his crib the whole night, she came home to find both girls dozing on the couch, and she said nothing when the rumor flew because her husband was on the council. She hands you her date book. "Somebody should finally read it."
success.art: A middle-aged woman in a pantsuit handing a small worn date book across a garage sale card table to a teenager, her eyes wet, a teenage boy watching from behind a crate of records

failure.text: Her smile clicks shut like a compact. "We don't talk about her in this house." Teddy mouths sorry. When you turn to go, there is a cranberry cardigan folded neatly on the card table, priced at twenty-five cents in someone else's handwriting.
failure.art: A neatly folded cranberry cable-knit cardigan on a garage sale card table with a handwritten price tag, two steel knitting needles crossed on top of it

choices.label: Help Teddy price records and ask about the old story

success.text: Teddy has heard the story his whole life: he is the baby who got lost. "Except I wasn't. Mom's date book says so. She just never showed anybody." He digs it out of the box and slides it to you between two Bee Gees records. "Somebody owes that girl."
success.art: Two teenagers sitting cross-legged on a driveway among crates of vinyl records, one sliding a small worn date book across to the other, afternoon sun on the garage door

failure.text: Teddy shrugs. "I was a baby. Supposedly I almost died. Thanks, Mom." He walks off. In the record crate, every album has the same sleeve on top: a 1971 Creature Feature station promo, two girls' initials scratched into the corner.
failure.art: A crate of vinyl records on a driveway, the front sleeve a faded 1971 late-night monster movie promo with two sets of initials scratched into one corner

clues.title: The Harvest Hop negative
clues.hint: Mickey Moore is missing from the 1972 Glimmer Falls High yearbook, but the yearbook office keeps every negative it ever shot.

encounter.title: Not Pictured
encounter.place: Yearbook office darkroom, Glimmer Falls High
encounter.text: The 1972 yearbook lists MICHAELA MOORE, NOT PICTURED, beside a gray square. In the darkroom closet, a binder of negatives from the 1971 Harvest Hop has one strip pulled halfway out of its sleeve. Hold it to the red safelight and you can just make out two girls dancing cheek to cheek in matching knitted cardigans.
encounter.art: A small school darkroom glowing deep red under a safelight, developing trays on a counter, a teenager holding a strip of film negatives up to the red light, the tiny inverted image on one square of film showing two girls in matching knitted cardigans dancing cheek to cheek, clothespins and drying prints on a line overhead, deep red light, close medium shot

choices.label: Mix the chemicals and print the photo

success.text: The print blooms up through the developer tray: Mickey and June at the Harvest Hop, foreheads together, laughing too loud at something only they can hear. On the back of the negative sleeve, in looping ballpoint: Knit one, purl two, I'm crazy for you. Save me a dance every year. J.
success.art: A black-and-white photo emerging in a darkroom developer tray, two teenage girls in matching hand-knit cardigans dancing with their foreheads touching, laughing

failure.text: The print comes up black, then gray, then a single pale oval where a face should be. The safelight flickers. When it steadies, someone has drawn a smiley face on the darkroom door in fixer, still dripping.
failure.art: A photographic print floating in a darkroom tray showing a single blank pale oval face, a dripping smiley face drawn on a red-lit darkroom door behind it

choices.label: Show the negative to Coach Pruitt, who has been here forever

success.text: Coach Pruitt was in her first year at Glimmer Falls in 1971. She holds the negative to the window a long time. "Best shortstop I ever had. Knit the whole infield scarves." She pulls a team photo from her office wall with Mickey in it, and June beside her, and their two hands not quite hidden behind a glove.
success.art: A tall broad-shouldered softball coach in a track jacket holding a film negative up to a sunny office window, a 1971 girls' softball team photo on the desk in front of a teenager

failure.text: Coach Pruitt is mid-practice and tells you to run two laps for loitering in the darkroom. On the second lap you glance up at the bleachers. A figure in a cardigan is sitting very still in the top row, knitting, watching only you.
failure.art: A teenager jogging around an empty school track at dusk, a still figure in a pale mask and cardigan sitting alone at the top of the bleachers, knitting

signature.title: The Babysitter Answers the Phone
signature.place: The Quintero house, babysitting, Sunday night
signature.text: The Quintero twins are finally asleep and the Creature Feature is on. At 9:41 the kitchen wall phone rings. On the line, nobody speaks. There is only a slow click, click, click, like knitting needles, and then a girl's soft voice: "A good sitter doesn't tie up the line." Across the street, under the streetlight, a pale face is watching the window. You blink, and the streetlight is empty.
signature.art: A teenage babysitter in a dim 1980s kitchen at 9:41 at night holding a yellow wall phone with a long curly cord, a television glowing in the next room, and through the window over the sink a tall young woman in a long cranberry cable-knit cardigan with loose auburn curls and a pale blank plaster mask standing perfectly still under a streetlight across the road, steel knitting needles held low at her side, cold streetlight and warm TV glow, medium shot

choices.label: Hang up and lock every door and window

success.text: Front door, back door, slider, the window over the sink. You reach the dog door last and slam the bolt just as the flap starts to lift. It settles. Footsteps cross the lawn, unhurried. At dawn there is a tiny knitted mitten on the mat, exactly the size of a baby's hand.
success.art: A teenager sliding a bolt across a kitchen dog door, the rubber flap pressed inward, and in a second moment a tiny knitted cranberry mitten on a doormat at dawn

failure.text: Every lock is already locked, from the inside, except the back door, which is standing open. The phone cord has been knitted into a tight, neat cable stitch, and the twins are both awake, whispering about the nice lady in the yard.
failure.art: A yellow phone cord tightly knitted into a cable stitch hanging from a kitchen wall, a back door standing open onto a dark yard, two small kids in pajamas peeking from a hallway

choices.label: Stay on the line and talk to her

success.text: You tell her the twins are asleep, the dishes are done, and the second movie is about a fish man. The clicking slows. "I did the dishes too," the voice whispers, sixteen and so tired. "Nobody ever wrote that down." The line goes quiet, gently, like a phone set back in its cradle.
success.art: A teenager sitting on a kitchen floor with a wall phone receiver pressed to one ear, listening intently, a clean dish rack beside them, warm lamp light and a calm quiet house

failure.text: "Hello? Who is this?" you say, too loud. The clicking stops. Then every phone in the house rings at once, upstairs and down, and they do not stop until you pull every cord out of every wall.
failure.art: A frantic teenager yanking a phone cord out of a wall jack in a dark hallway, three different phones ringing on side tables around them

choices.label: Drop the phone and run upstairs to the twins

success.text: The twins are asleep, a stuffed dinosaur each. You sit between their beds all night with a flashlight and every light on. Once, the hall floor creaks and stops at the door, and you say, out loud, "They're fine. I've got them." The creaking goes away.
success.art: A teenager sitting on the floor between two small beds in a kids' bedroom holding a flashlight, two sleeping children hugging stuffed dinosaurs, a long shadow in the hallway doorway

failure.text: You take the stairs two at a time and trip on a skein of cranberry yarn stretched across the top step. You land hard. The twins sleep through it. The dangling phone downstairs is still clicking.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled at the top of a carpeted staircase tangled in a strand of cranberry yarn, a phone receiver dangling by its cord in the dark kitchen below

signature.title: The Couple on the Couch
signature.place: A Halloween-week party on Pinecone Lane
signature.text: Somebody's parents are in Reno, so half of Glimmer Falls High is in their rec room. Two of your friends are sharing the plaid couch and a bowl of popcorn, holding hands under an afghan, finally. Through the sliding glass door, past a clothesline of white sheets in the backyard, a pale blank face is watching them. When the sheets flap, she is one sheet closer.
signature.art: A wood-paneled 1980s rec room party at night, two teenagers holding hands on a plaid couch under a crocheted afghan with a bowl of popcorn, other kids dancing behind them, and through the sliding glass door a dark backyard clothesline of white sheets with a tall figure in a cranberry cardigan and a pale blank plaster mask standing among them, a teenager at the slider looking out, lamp light inside and blue night outside, medium wide shot

choices.label: Get the couple and everyone else upstairs, now

success.text: You haul the couch couple up by their wrists and the whole party stampedes after you into the upstairs bathroom, twelve kids and a bowl of popcorn in the tub. Out the little window, the Shape stands on the lawn and tilts her head, as if she has never seen anyone protect a couple before.
success.art: A crowd of teenagers crammed into a pink-tiled upstairs bathroom, several standing in the tub with a popcorn bowl, one peering out a small window at a masked figure tilting her head on the moonlit lawn below

failure.text: You run for the slider to lock it and the sheets on the line seem to reach for you. You go down in a tangle of wet cotton, wrestling the laundry, while somewhere close by a pair of needles goes click.
failure.art: A teenager tangled and struggling in white sheets fallen from a backyard clothesline at night, a pair of steel knitting needles glinting in the grass nearby

choices.label: Hit every light, crank the stereo and call couples skate

success.text: Every lamp, the porch light, the lava lamp. You put on the slowest song on the tape and yell "Couples skate!" in socks on the linoleum, and suddenly everyone is dancing with everyone. The Shape stands in the bright yard a long while, watching a room where nobody is alone, and then she is simply gone.
success.art: A brightly lit rec room full of teenagers slow dancing in socks on linoleum under a glowing lava lamp, a porch-lit backyard outside the sliding door holding an empty clothesline of sheets

failure.text: The stereo shrieks and dies. So does every light in the house. In the dark, the couch springs creak as two people stand up fast, and on the glass of the slider a hand writes in fog: LIGHTS OUT BY TEN.
failure.art: A dark rec room lit only by moonlight, foggy writing traced by a finger on a sliding glass door, frightened teenagers huddled on a plaid couch

choices.label: Step outside and walk straight up to her

success.text: You cross the wet lawn with your flashlight on her mask. Up close it is plaster, homemade, with a girl's fingerprints pressed into the cheeks where someone shaped it too hard. She raises one needle, slowly, and points it down the hill toward Crystal Street. Toward the Kettering house. Then the sheets flap and she is gone.
success.art: A teenager on a dark wet lawn shining a flashlight on a pale plaster mask pressed with faint fingerprints, the masked figure in a cardigan pointing one knitting needle down a hill toward distant suburban lights

failure.text: The sheets flap and she is gone. They flap again and she is behind you, close enough that you hear the yarn sliding through her fingers. You run inside, slam the slider, and nobody will sit on that couch for the rest of the night.
failure.art: A pale masked figure in a cardigan standing directly behind a frightened teenager on a moonlit lawn, white sheets billowing on a clothesline around them

signature.title: I'll Be Right Back
signature.place: The Delgado house, co-sitting with a friend, after dark
signature.text: You and Tina Vasquez are co-sitting the Delgado kids, who are asleep upstairs under a night-light shaped like a moon. Tina spills a whole bowl of buttered popcorn down her shirt and stands up. "There's a washer in the garage," she says. "I'll be right back." The garage door closes behind her. The washing machine starts, thump, thump, thump. Five minutes. Ten. On the kitchen counter the phone cord has begun to sway by itself, and from somewhere very close comes a slow click, click, click.
signature.art: A dim 1980s suburban kitchen at night, a yellow wall phone on the wall with its curly cord swaying by itself, a closed door to the garage with light under it and a washing machine thumping behind it, a teenager on the living room couch with a bowl of spilled buttered popcorn turning toward the door, a moon-shaped night-light glowing at the top of the stairs, single stove light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Grab the flashlight and go after her

success.text: You open the garage onto a wall of soap bubbles and Tina, perfectly fine and absolutely furious, standing on top of the dryer. "Somebody knitted the door shut," she hisses. The inside knob is wrapped in neat cranberry rows. You cut her loose with the kitchen scissors. In the driveway, a pale shape watches the two of you walk back inside together, and slowly lowers her needles.
success.art: A teenager with a flashlight in a garage overflowing with soap bubbles, a furious friend standing on top of a dryer, a doorknob wrapped in neat cranberry knitting, a pale masked figure in a cardigan watching from the dark driveway

failure.text: The garage is dark and full of thumping. Your flashlight finds the washer, the dryer, a rake, and then a pale mask at the side window, inches from the glass, which is exactly when Tina taps you on the shoulder from behind. You both scream loud enough to wake the block, the Delgado kids included.
failure.art: A teenager's flashlight beam landing on a pale plaster mask pressed close to a dark garage window, a friend tapping their shoulder from behind, both mid-scream, a rumbling washing machine beside them

choices.label: Call everyone into the living room: new rule, everybody stays together

success.text: You hand out walkie-talkies, carry the sleeping kids down in their blankets and drag Tina back from the garage door by her popcorn-stained sleeve. Everybody stays in one room. At the window, the shape outside tilts her head at the sight, the way a sitter does when she finds the kids already tucked in, and walks on down the street.
success.art: A cozy living room with sleeping kids bundled in blankets on the couch, two teenagers holding walkie-talkies beside them, through the window a pale masked figure in a cardigan tilting her head under a streetlight

failure.text: By the time you have everyone together, you count heads and come up one short. Tina went for the garage after all, and the big garage door is rumbling up on its own, slow as a theatre curtain, onto a driveway lit by one streetlight. She is fine. Neither of you sleeps.
failure.art: A garage door slowly rising by itself onto a dark driveway lit by a single streetlight, a startled teenager standing in the garage in a popcorn-stained shirt, a friend peering from the kitchen doorway

choices.label: Shout the oldest rule in the horror-movie book after her

success.text: "You can't say I'll be right back!" you holler. "It's the first rule!" Tina freezes in the doorway, considers it, and walks back to the couch, shirt and all. "Fine. But you're watching me eat popcorn off myself." Out on the lawn the pale shape stands very still, like someone hearing a rule she has never heard before: one that keeps a girl alive.
success.art: Two teenagers laughing on a plaid couch, one picking popcorn off her shirt, a camcorder and horror videotapes on the coffee table, through the window a pale masked figure standing very still on the moonlit lawn

failure.text: Tina laughs and says it again, louder, on purpose: "I'll be right back!" The lights go out. When they come back on, you are both locked in the garage with a washer full of popcorn shirt, and the inside knob has been knitted shut in tidy cranberry rows.
failure.art: Two teenagers locked in a dim garage beside a rumbling washing machine, one tugging at a doorknob wrapped tight in neat cranberry knitting, a bare bulb swinging overhead

signature.title: Behind the Hedge
signature.place: Walking home down Crystal Street at dusk
signature.text: You are walking home from school with Benny Bautista, who is talking about the Pine Ridge game and not looking where you are looking. A pale face in a cranberry cardigan is standing behind the Hendersons' hedge, perfectly still. You blink and there is only hedge. Two houses later she is beside a parked station wagon. "There's no such thing as the boogeyman," Benny says, without turning around. Up ahead, beside the next hedge, a pale shape is waiting, and your house is still four doors away.
signature.art: A suburban street at dusk lined with trimmed hedges and fallen orange leaves, two teenagers walking home with backpacks, one boy in a team jacket talking with his hands, the other glancing nervously ahead at a tall figure in a long cranberry cardigan with loose auburn curls and a pale blank plaster mask standing perfectly still beside a hedge farther down the sidewalk, long low orange sunlight, wide shot

choices.label: Snap an instant photo of her so Benny has to believe you

success.text: The flash pops. Benny laughs at you right up until the photo develops in his hand: the Hendersons' hedge and, beside it, crisp and clear, a girl in a plaster mask and a hand-knit cardigan, feet together like she is waiting for school picture day. Benny goes pale and quiet. When you both look up, the hedge is just a hedge, and he walks you all the way to your door.
success.art: A pale wide-eyed teenage boy holding an instant photo showing a masked girl in a hand-knit cardigan beside a hedge, his friend holding the camera, the real hedge beside them in the dusk light

failure.text: The flash pops, and the photo develops into a picture of you, from behind, taken a moment ago from somewhere very close. Benny stops laughing. You both run the last four houses and slam your front door, and the photo lies face-up on the welcome mat all night where you dropped it.
failure.art: An instant photo lying on a doormat in porch light showing a teenager from behind on a dusky sidewalk, shot from very close, two teenagers peeking out through a front door window

choices.label: Walk straight up to the hedge and look behind it

success.text: You part the branches. Behind the hedge is a strip of lawn, a garden gnome, and a skein of cranberry yarn wound neatly around a stake, tidy as a sitter's workbasket. Tied on top with a bow is a paper tag in round, careful handwriting: Home by dark. You realize she wasn't stalking you. She was making sure you got home.
success.art: A teenager parting the branches of a hedge at dusk to find a garden gnome and a neat skein of cranberry yarn wound around a wooden stake, tied with a small paper tag and a bow

failure.text: You part the branches and she is right there, a plaster face an inch from yours, the eyeholes dark. Neither of you moves. Then Benny yells your name, you flinch, and when you look back the hedge is just a hedge, and your jacket's zipper pull has been replaced with a tiny knitted pom-pom.
failure.art: A teenager frozen nose to nose with a pale plaster mask between parted hedge branches at dusk, a tiny cranberry knitted pom-pom dangling from the zipper of their jacket

choices.label: Wave and call "Happy Halloween!" like she's any other neighbor

success.text: "Evening! Happy Halloween!" you call, cheerful as a mail carrier. The pale shape behind the hedge stands still for a long, long time. Then one hand rises, stiffly, and waves back, exactly the way a polite girl waves at the neighbors when her mother is watching. "Who are you waving at?" Benny asks. You don't answer. You are trying to remember the last time anyone said hello to her.
success.art: A teenager on a dusky suburban sidewalk waving cheerfully toward a hedge, a pale masked figure in a cranberry cardigan raising one stiff hand to wave back, a puzzled friend looking the wrong way

failure.text: Your wave comes out shaky and your voice cracks halfway through Halloween. The shape tilts her head, as if correcting your posture. All the way home, every hedge you pass rustles once, politely, in the order you pass it, and your porch light is already on when you get there, though the house is dark.
failure.art: A nervous teenager hurrying down a dark suburban sidewalk past a row of rustling hedges, a single porch light glowing over the front steps of a dark house at the end of the street

signature.title: Stay With Your Group
signature.place: The Jaycees Haunted House in the old Thriftco on Route 49
signature.text: The Jaycees Haunted House fills the dead Thriftco on Route 49 with plywood hallways, fog machines and dads in rubber masks. A hand-painted board at the entrance lists the house rules: STAY WITH YOUR GROUP. NO RUNNING. NO SCREAMING. In the Babysitter Room, a set with a plaid couch and a wall phone, a volunteer in a white mask and a cardigan lies face down on the carpet as a prop. Your group walks past. You look back. The prop is sitting up, head tilted, counting you with one steel needle.
signature.art: A cheap plywood haunted house built inside an old dime store, a fake living room set with a plaid couch and a yellow wall phone, fog curling across the carpet under red and green bulbs, a tall figure in a cranberry cardigan and a pale blank plaster mask sitting up from the floor with her head tilted and one steel knitting needle raised to count, a group of teenagers walking past in a line holding hands, the last one looking back, low fog light, wide shot

choices.label: Topple a rack of rubber bats on her and run for it

success.text: The rack comes down in a rubbery avalanche and buries her to the shoulders. You herd your whole group through three rooms at a dead sprint, breaking two house rules at once, and burst out the emergency exit into the parking lot. When you look back through the door she is sitting up again among the bats, head tilted, watching you go.
success.art: A pale masked figure in a cardigan buried to the shoulders in a heap of rubber bats on a haunted house floor, teenagers bursting through a glowing emergency exit into a dark parking lot

failure.text: The rack wobbles and stays put. You turn to run and she is already standing, right behind you, close enough that you smell the cedar chest on her cardigan. You run anyway, straight into a fog machine, and come out the far side alone in the Mad Scientist Room.
failure.art: A frightened teenager stumbling out of thick fog into a haunted house mad scientist lab set with bubbling plastic beakers, a pale masked figure in a cardigan looming in the haze behind them

choices.label: Find the breaker box and flip on the store's old fluorescent lights

success.text: Behind a plywood tombstone you find the old Thriftco breaker panel and throw every switch. The fluorescents stutter on, humming, and the haunted house becomes a cheap maze of painted plywood and embarrassed dads. In the bald white light the figure in the cardigan raises her hands against the glare, steps back into the one dark hallway left, and is gone.
success.art: Harsh fluorescent tube lights flickering on over a maze of painted plywood walls, embarrassed dads in rubber masks blinking, a pale masked figure in a cardigan shielding her face and backing into a shadowy hallway

failure.text: The switch you throw is the one marked SPECIAL EFFECTS. Every strobe, fog machine and recorded scream in the building goes off at once, and in each strobe flash the shape in the cardigan is one room closer, until the volunteers evacuate and you wait in the parking lot with your heart in your throat.
failure.art: A haunted house corridor exploding with strobe lights and billowing fog, a pale masked figure in a cardigan caught mid-step in a strobe flash, a teenager gripping an old breaker panel

choices.label: Link everyone hand in hand and walk through slowly, counting heads out loud

success.text: "One, two, three, four," you count, and your group counts back. Everyone walks. Everyone stays quiet. You cross the whole house in a chain, and the shape in the cardigan follows at a careful sitter's distance, the way you trail a line of little kids home from the bus stop. At the exit she stops on the threshold, and very softly, she finishes the count: "All here."
success.art: A chain of teenagers holding hands walking slowly through a foggy haunted house corridor, a pale masked figure in a cardigan following at a careful distance behind them like a babysitter counting heads

failure.text: The chain breaks in the fog room when somebody's hand slips. When you count again you come up one short, and you have to go back in alone, through every room, calling a name while a pair of needles clicks somewhere in the dark. The missing kid turns out to be outside already, eating a caramel apple.
failure.art: A lone teenager calling into a dark foggy haunted house hallway lit by a red bulb, a pair of steel knitting needles glinting in the shadows ahead

signature.title: The Girl Who Laughs Too Loud
signature.place: Mischief Night skate, Pump Iron roller rink annex
signature.text: It is Mischief Night, the disco ball is spinning, and somebody tells a joke so bad you laugh until you snort. The music cuts out. Under the strobe light, between one flash and the next, a pale shape in a cardigan is standing in the middle of the rink without skates. Every flash, she is closer. She is walking toward whoever laughed the loudest, and that was you.
signature.art: A crowded 1980s roller rink on Mischief Night under a spinning disco ball and white strobe flashes, skaters frozen mid-glide, a tall figure in a long cranberry cardigan and a pale blank plaster mask standing on the wooden floor in plain sneakers, walking toward one teenager at the rail who still has a hand over their mouth from laughing, stark strobe light and colored rink lights, wide shot

choices.label: Duck into the skate-rental closet and hold your breath

success.text: You squeeze in behind racks of brown rental skates and pull the slatted door shut. Through the slats you see her stop. A steel needle slides between two slats, an inch from your eye, and holds there. Then, very softly, she knits one row on it, and walks away.
success.art: View from inside a dark slatted closet full of rental roller skates, a single steel knitting needle poking between the slats, a pale masked figure blurred beyond the door

failure.text: The closet door does not quite close. A needle hooks your sleeve through the gap and tugs, once, like a teacher fixing a collar. You tumble out onto the rink floor in a landslide of skates as the lights come up.
failure.art: A teenager tumbling out of a rental closet onto a wooden roller rink floor in an avalanche of brown skates, a strand of cranberry yarn caught on their sleeve

choices.label: Laugh louder, and get the whole rink laughing with you

success.text: You laugh like a hyena and point at the next person until they crack, and they point at the next, and in thirty seconds the whole rink is howling. She cannot pick one loud laugh out of a building full of them. She stands still in the strobe, and for a moment her shoulders shake too.
success.art: A whole roller rink crowd doubled over laughing under a disco ball, a pale masked figure in a cardigan standing still in the middle with her shoulders lifted as if laughing

failure.text: Your laugh comes out thin and alone and dies in the silence. She is right in front of you now. She raises one finger to the lips of the mask. Shh. Then the strobe flashes and she is gone, and you cannot make a sound until morning.
failure.art: A pale blank mask inches from a frightened teenager's face, one finger raised to its lips, strobe light flashing across a silent roller rink

choices.label: Grab a rink broom and knock the needles out of her hands

success.text: Crack. The needles skitter across the floor, spinning under the disco ball. She looks at her empty hands like she has forgotten what they are for. She picks the needles up one at a time, very carefully, and walks out through the fire door into the dark.
success.art: Two steel knitting needles skittering across a wooden roller rink floor under a disco ball, a masked figure looking down at her empty hands, a teenager gripping a broom

failure.text: She catches the broom without looking and snaps it like a pretzel stick. The halves clatter on the floor. You back away across the rink on wobbling ankles while she follows, one calm step at a time, until the lights come up.
failure.art: A pale masked figure holding the two halves of a snapped broom on a roller rink floor, a teenager backing away on wobbly skates under strobe lights

signature.title: The Babysitter Pledge
signature.place: St. Jude's church basement, the Halloween Safety Committee sitter meeting, 8 p.m.
signature.text: Somebody signed you up for the Halloween Safety Committee's sitter meeting, so you are in a folding chair in St. Jude's basement holding a Babysitter Pledge card while Mrs. Carol Pickett reads the rules aloud in her orange sash. No boys in the house. No long phone calls. Lights out by ten. No laughing loud enough to wake the baby. In the very back row, past the coffee urn, a girl in a cranberry cardigan sits perfectly still, knitting. Every time Mrs. Pickett reads a rule, the needles click once, like a gavel, and the fluorescent lights dim.
signature.art: A church basement at eight at night with rows of folding chairs, teenage babysitters holding small paper slips, a stern woman in an orange sash speaking at a podium beside a steaming coffee urn, and in the very back row a girl in a cranberry cardigan with a pale blank plaster mask sitting perfectly still and knitting, the fluorescent tubes overhead dimming, a teenager turning around in their chair, flat greenish light, wide shot

choices.label: Stand up and propose a new rule for the pledge, with feeling

success.text: "Point of order!" you announce, and propose Rule Eleven: every sitter laughs out loud at least once a night. The room giggles. Pearl Washington, rocking in a lawn chair she brought from home, seconds the motion. Mrs. Pickett sputters, and the room votes yes by a landslide. In the back row, the needles stop. When you look, the chair is vacant, and on it lies a pledge card with your new rule copied neatly at the bottom in round, careful handwriting.
success.art: A teenager standing in a church basement proposing a motion with one raised finger, rows of babysitters laughing, an elderly woman in a lawn chair seconding it, a vacant back-row chair holding a small card and a ball of cranberry yarn

failure.text: You stand up to propose a new rule and every head turns, including the one in the back row. Your mouth goes dry. Mrs. Pickett says, "Sit down, dear," and you do, and for the rest of the meeting you can feel a plaster stare on the back of your neck and hear the needles keeping time.
failure.art: A nervous teenager sinking into a folding chair at a church basement meeting, a woman in an orange sash at the podium, a pale plaster-masked girl in a cranberry cardigan staring from the back row

choices.label: Carry two cups of coffee to the back row and sit beside the knitting girl

success.text: You sit down beside her and set the second cup of terrible church coffee on the chair between you. She keeps her smooth plaster face turned toward the front, but her needles slow. After the next rule, very quietly, she says, "I signed one of those in 1971. I kept every rule but one." When the lights come up, the second cup is half gone and wearing a tiny knitted cozy.
success.art: A teenager sitting in the back row of a church basement beside a pale plaster-masked girl in a cranberry cardigan, two paper cups of coffee on the chair between them, one wearing a tiny knitted cozy

failure.text: You sit down beside her and the folding chair collapses under you with a bang that echoes off the cinderblock. The whole basement turns to look. When you scramble up, the back row is vacant, and your pledge card has been knitted neatly into the seat of your chair.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled on the floor of a church basement among the pieces of a collapsed folding chair, rows of babysitters turning to stare, cranberry yarn draped over a vacant back-row chair

choices.label: Raise your hand and ask Mrs. Pickett who wrote these rules

success.text: "Who wrote these?" you ask, all innocence. Mrs. Pickett opens her mouth and nothing comes out. Her hand drifts to her sash. "They're just common sense, dear. Every good girl knows them." Down the rows, a few sitters trade looks, and you watch Mrs. Pickett's eyes flick to the back row and away, fast, the way people glance at something they have spent fifteen years not looking at.
success.art: A woman in an orange sash at a church basement podium touching her sash nervously, a teenager with a raised hand among the rows, babysitters glancing toward a shadowy back row

failure.text: "Who wrote these?" you ask, and the lights die. In the dark, every pledge card in the basement rustles at once, and a girl's voice right beside your ear whispers, "Rules are rules." When the custodian finds the breaker, your card has a new line stitched across the bottom in cranberry yarn: Don't ask.
failure.art: A dark church basement lit by a single flashlight beam, rows of folding chairs, small cards fluttering in the air, a pale plaster mask glimpsed close beside a startled teenager's ear

signature.title: Practice a Pleasant Expression
signature.place: The art room at Glimmer Falls High, after the late bus
signature.text: You go back to the art room for your backpack after the late bus and find the plaster masks from Mr. Quintero's sculpture unit drying on the shelves: thirty white faces of kids you know, every one smiling the same small, polite, practiced smile. So is the one with your name under it, though you never made one. At the teacher's desk sits a girl in a cranberry cardigan and a plaster mask, tapping a steel needle on the desk like a ruler. "Again," she says, in the voice of every grown-up who ever told a girl to smile. "Practice a pleasant expression."
signature.art: A dim high school art room after the late bus, shelves of thirty white plaster face masks drying in rows, all smiling the same small polite smile, a girl in a cranberry cardigan with a pale blank plaster mask sitting at the teacher's desk tapping a steel knitting needle on the desktop, a teenager with a backpack frozen in the doorway, cold window light from the dusk outside, medium wide shot

choices.label: Make the ugliest, silliest face of your life, right at her

success.text: You cross your eyes, stretch your mouth with both pinkies and stick out your tongue as far as it goes. Then the fish. Then the gorilla. Along the shelves, thirty plaster masks crack, pop and grin, gap-toothed and goofy, every one a different face. The girl at the desk drops her needle. In the morning the whole school crowds into the art room to see the masks that made themselves funny, and Mr. Quintero gives everybody an A.
success.art: A teenager making a ridiculous cross-eyed face in a dim art room, shelves of white plaster masks cracking into goofy grins, a pale masked girl in a cranberry cardigan dropping a knitting needle

failure.text: You try to make a face, but it comes out stiff, then small, then polite. Your cheeks lock into the practiced smile and stay that way all the way home, through dinner and into homeroom, where three different teachers tell you how pleasant you look today.
failure.art: A teenager at a breakfast table wearing a stiff polite smile, a plate of eggs untouched, family members glancing at each other across the kitchen in morning light

choices.label: Ask her gently who made her practice

success.text: "Who made you practice?" you ask. The tapping stops. "Valley Haven," she says at last. "Deportment class. They pressed plaster on our faces and made us hold still until it set. Smiling." She touches the cheek of her mask, where a girl's fingerprints are pressed in too deep. "I was sixteen. I wasn't sorry for anything." She turns the mask with your name face down on the desk, gently, like she is letting you off the hook.
success.art: A pale girl in a cranberry cardigan at a teacher's desk touching the fingerprint dents in the cheek of her plaster mask, a teenager sitting across from her listening in a dim art room

failure.text: "Who made you practice?" you ask, and she tilts her head the way a teacher does right before detention. "You did," she says. "All of you. Every time you said smile." The masks on the shelves turn to face you one by one, and you back out into a hallway that is very long and very dark.
failure.art: A long dark high school hallway at night, a teenager backing away from an art room where rows of white plaster masks have all turned to face them

choices.label: Take the mask with your name off the shelf and break it on the floor

success.text: You lift the plaster face with your name under it, raise it over your head and bring it down on the linoleum. It shatters like a dropped plate. The sound rings through the empty school, and every other mask on the shelves cracks down the middle in sympathy. The girl at the desk stands, very slowly, and looks at the pieces for a long time, like she has wanted to do that for fifteen years.
success.art: A teenager smashing a white plaster mask on an art room floor, shards flying, shelves of masks cracking down the middle, a pale masked girl in a cranberry cardigan rising slowly behind the desk

failure.text: The plaster is harder than it looks. It bounces off the linoleum without a scratch and lands face up, smiling at you. When you bend to grab it, the girl from the desk is already standing over you, handing it back like a lost assignment. You take it home. In the morning it is on your pillow.
failure.art: A smiling white plaster mask resting on a pillow in a dark bedroom at dawn, a teenager sitting bolt upright in bed staring at it

signature.title: Every Sitter on the Block
signature.place: Crystal Street, Mischief Night, a babysitter in every house
signature.text: Every parent on Crystal Street has gone to the Jaycees' costume ball, so every house on the cul-de-sac has a sitter tonight, and you are one of them. At 9:30 the walkie-talkies start crackling: a figure on the Hendersons' lawn, then by the Okafors' mailbox, then under your streetlight. The Shape is walking the circle of houses, needles in hand, stopping at each lit window to count what she sees: a sitter on the phone, a boyfriend on the couch, a girl laughing too loud. Eight houses. Eight sitters. Twenty-three sleeping kids. She is checking every rule on every one.
signature.art: A suburban cul-de-sac on a misty autumn night, every house glowing with lit windows showing teenage babysitters inside, one on the phone, a couple on a couch, a girl laughing, a teenager on a porch holding a walkie-talkie, and a tall figure in a cranberry cardigan with a pale blank plaster mask walking the curving sidewalk with knitting needles held low, stopping at a lit window, mist around the streetlights, wide shot

choices.label: Call every sitter and every kid out to the roundabout for a Mischief Night block party

success.text: Over the walkie-talkies you call it: "Everybody out! Flashlights, blankets, snacks, bring the babies!" Ten minutes later the roundabout is a block party, eight sitters and twenty-three kids in pajamas around the Heartstone, a boombox playing, everyone breaking every rule at once and all of them together. The Shape stands at the edge of the light, counting, and keeps getting the same number. Everyone. At last she sits down on the curb to watch.
success.art: A cheerful block party around a glowing purple geode at night, teenage babysitters and children in pajamas with flashlights and blankets, a boombox, a pale masked girl in a cranberry cardigan sitting on the curb watching

failure.text: Half the sitters come out. The other half lock their doors and will not answer, and you spend the night running between the party and the dark porches while needles click behind every hedge. Everyone is fine by midnight. You are not sure your heart is.
failure.art: A teenager running between dark suburban porches at night clutching a walkie-talkie, a glowing roundabout party in the distance, knitting needles glinting behind a hedge

choices.label: Run a walkie-talkie roll call: every house checks in, every ten minutes

success.text: You run roll call on channel nine like an air-traffic controller. "House three, check in." "House three, all good, Jamie's asleep." "House six?" Every ten minutes, again and again. Out on the street the Shape stops at each window and hears a sitter reporting that the kids are safe, and you watch her nod once at every house, as if checking it off a list.
success.art: A teenager on a porch speaking into a walkie-talkie under a porch light, lit rooms all around a cul-de-sac with babysitters answering on their own radios, a pale masked girl nodding beside a lit house

failure.text: At the 10:20 check-in, house five does not answer. You sprint over. The sitter is fine (she dropped her walkie in the toilet), but by the time you get back, every walkie on the street is playing the same slow click, click, click.
failure.art: A teenager sprinting across a dark lawn toward a lit house at night, a crackling walkie-talkie in hand, a pale cardigan-clad shape at the edge of a streetlight

choices.label: Walk the circle of houses yourself, ten paces behind her, flashlight on

success.text: You fall in step ten paces behind her, flashlight steady. She stops at a window; you stop. She goes on; you go on. At the last house she turns and looks at you for a long time, and you realize you have been doing exactly what she is doing: counting everyone, checking every window, making sure. She lowers her needles and walks on, and at the next window she passes, she does not stop.
success.art: A teenager with a flashlight walking ten paces behind a pale masked girl in a cranberry cardigan along a misty suburban sidewalk at night, her knitting needles lowered, lit houses glowing on both sides

failure.text: She stops. You stop. She turns around, and you drop the flashlight. By the time you find it rolling in the gutter she is gone, every porch light on the street has switched off at once, and you walk the rest of the circle in the dark, calling the sitters' names.
failure.art: A teenager alone on a pitch-dark suburban street at night, a flashlight rolling in the gutter, every porch light dark, a ball of cranberry yarn unspooling across the asphalt

finale.title: Halloween at the Kettering House
finale.text: At 11:40 on Halloween night every phone on Crystal Street starts ringing at once. Your crew is barricaded in the Kettering living room with the same plaid couch and the same wall phone from 1971. Out in the street, the Shape walks down the center line between the jack-o'-lanterns, needles in hand, and stops at the front walk. Carol Pickett, who was Carol Lund, stands frozen on the sidewalk in her Halloween Safety Committee sash. The mask turns toward her, then toward you. "Rules are rules," says every phone in every house.
finale.art: A split-level suburban house on Halloween night with every window lit and teens peering out from the living room, a plaid couch visible inside, jack-o'-lanterns lining the street, a tall young woman in a long cranberry cable-knit cardigan with loose auburn curls and a pale blank plaster mask standing on the front walk holding steel knitting needles low, a woman in an orange safety sash frozen on the sidewalk, cold streetlight and orange jack-o'-lantern glow, wide shot

choices.label: Hold the stairs and drive her off the balcony

success.text: She comes up the stairs one calm step at a time and you meet her at the top with everything you have. The railing gives. She goes over the balcony into the leaf pile on the lawn below. When you all lean over to look, the leaves are empty except for the shape of a girl pressed into them.
success.art: A teenager with a baseball bat at the top of a staircase beside a broken balcony railing, below on the moonlit lawn a pile of autumn leaves holding the empty pressed outline of a person

failure.text: She does not hurry and she does not stop. The bat bounces off the cardigan like you swung at a cloud. A needle pins your sleeve to the banister, neat as a sewing pin, and she walks on past you toward your friends.
failure.art: A teenager's jacket sleeve pinned to a wooden banister by a steel knitting needle, a pale masked figure walking past them down a dark upstairs hallway

choices.label: Stage a final-girl ending straight out of Zelda's movies

success.text: Zelda lets loose the scream that ended The Thing from Crystal Springs, the decoy in the borrowed cardigan slumps just inside the hall closet, and the Shape goes for it like every slasher in every picture. The moment she steps in after it, you slam the slatted door and wedge it with the couch. "Every monster falls for the third act," Zelda says.
success.alone: You let loose the scream that ended The Thing from Crystal Springs, the one you've rewound a hundred times, the decoy in the borrowed cardigan slumps just inside the hall closet, and the Shape goes for it like every slasher in every picture. The moment she steps in after it, you slam the slatted door and wedge it with the couch. Every monster falls for the third act.
success.art: A silver-haired older woman screaming theatrically in a living room while teenagers shove a plaid couch against a slatted hall closet door, a dummy in a cardigan slumped inside the closet

failure.text: She walks straight past the decoy and does not even turn her head. She has seen this movie. She has been in this movie for fifteen years. The closet door swings open on its own, and it is you she steps toward.
failure.art: A pale masked figure walking past a decoy dummy slumped in a hall closet doorway toward a frightened teenager, the slatted closet door swinging open behind her

choices.label: Answer the phone together and tell her what really happened

success.text: You pick up the wall phone and your whole crew crowds around the receiver. You read her Doris's date book: Teddy asleep, dishes done. You play Carol's voice off the Party Line tape. You hold the Harvest Hop photo up to the window. On the sidewalk, Carol Pickett starts to cry and says it out loud, for the whole street to hear: "I saw you kiss her. I made up the rest. I'm sorry, Mickey." The needles lower. Slowly, the Shape reaches up and takes off the mask.
success.art: A crowd of teens around a kitchen wall phone holding up an old dance photograph and a small date book to the window, outside a woman in a safety sash weeping on the sidewalk, a young woman in a cardigan lifting a pale mask from her freckled face

failure.text: Every phone keeps ringing over your words. She cannot hear the truth through fifteen years of rules and static. You have everything you need in your hands, but she needs it louder, clearer, from more than one voice.
failure.art: A teen shouting into a wall phone in a lit kitchen, an old photo and date book clutched in one hand, the pale masked figure outside the window unmoving in the static-blue streetlight

choices.label: Give her a better sitter rule, the way the first nights taught you

success.text: The first nights of the week taught you how the Shape thinks: she does not break rules, she enforces them. So you give her a better one. You lean out the Kettering front door and call it down the walk the way a head sitter calls it: "New rule! Nobody gets left alone tonight. Not the sitters, not the couple, not Mrs. Pickett. Everybody stays together." Your crew pulls Carol Pickett up onto the porch with the rest of you. The Shape stops at the foot of the walk, needles raised, counting face after face. Everyone together. Every rule kept. Slowly the needles come down, and all along Crystal Street the phones stop ringing.
success.art: A teenager leaning out the front entrance of a suburban house on Halloween night calling out, friends pulling a woman in an orange sash onto the porch, a pale masked girl in a cranberry cardigan lowering her knitting needles on the front walk

failure.text: You shout the new rule, but every phone on the street rings over you, and the Shape keeps walking up the path at the same calm pace. She has not heard your rule yet. The crew drags you back inside and slams the door, shaken but whole.
failure.art: Friends pulling a teenager back inside a suburban house on Halloween night, jack-o-lanterns lining the walk, a pale masked girl in a cranberry cardigan walking calmly up the path with needles raised

choices.label: Walk down the front walk and look her in the mask, the way you did all week

success.text: All week she watched you through sliding doors and hedges and from behind a teacher's desk, and all week you looked right back. You walk down the front walk between the jack-o'-lanterns and stop square between the Shape and Carol Pickett. "No," you say. "Not her. Not anybody. Nobody gets punished tonight." The needles rise and hold. You do not move. One by one your crew comes down the steps and stands with you, a wall of kids who refuse to be sorted into good and bad. The Shape lowers her needles, steps back off the walk and stands quietly under the streetlight, and the phones fall silent.
success.art: A row of teenagers standing shoulder to shoulder on a jack-o-lantern-lined front walk on Halloween night, a woman in an orange sash behind them, a pale masked girl in a cranberry cardigan lowering her needles under a streetlight

failure.text: You plant yourself on the walk, but your voice shakes and the needles do not even pause. She steps around you, calm as a crossing guard, and your crew has to yank Carol Pickett up the porch steps just ahead of her. You are fine. You are shaking. The night is not over.
failure.art: A shaking teenager on a front walk on Halloween night as a pale masked girl in a cranberry cardigan steps calmly past, friends hauling a woman in an orange sash up the porch steps

choices.label: Bring the whole street out like the night before Halloween, and let her count everyone safe

success.text: Last night, in a crowd where nobody got left behind, she counted and came up with the right number. So you open the Kettering door and bring the whole street out onto the lawn: sitters, couples, kids, the loud laughers, everyone under the porch lights. You read Doris's date book, play the Party Line tape and hold up the Harvest Hop photo, and then you hand Carol Pickett the phone. She says it for the whole street to hear: "I saw you kiss her. I made up the rest. I'm sorry, Mickey." The needles lower. The Shape counts the lawn one last time, everyone, all here, and slowly lifts her hands and takes off the mask.
success.art: A pale freckled teenage girl in a cranberry cardigan lifting away a plaster mask on a suburban lawn on Halloween night, neighbors, babysitters and kids gathered under glowing porch lights, a woman in an orange sash in tears holding a corded phone

failure.text: You bring the street out onto the lawn, but there are too many voices and too many phones ringing, and Carol freezes with the receiver in her hand. The Shape stands at the curb, counting and recounting, still waiting to hear the truth clearly enough to believe it.
failure.art: A crowded suburban lawn on Halloween night full of neighbors and kids, a woman in an orange sash frozen with a phone receiver on a long cord, a pale masked girl in a cranberry cardigan waiting at the curb

best.title: Everybody Survives the Night
best.text: Under the mask, Mickey Moore is just a freckled sixteen-year-old with a crooked smile. Mix puts Carol on the KGLM line and she tears up her Babysitter Pledge live on the air; Doris Kettering reads her date book from the porch; one by one, every porch light on Crystal Street blinks on and off, which is how this town says sorry. Nobody is punished. The couple stays on the couch, the sitters answer every phone, and the whole crew laughs too loud on purpose. At dawn Mickey finishes the last row of a long cranberry scarf, wraps it around your neck, and walks toward the Heartstone, where the light looks a lot like a porch light left on for a girl in a matching cardigan. The final girl was all of you.
best.art: Dawn on a suburban cul-de-sac strewn with burnt-out jack-o'-lanterns, every porch light glowing, a crowd of laughing teens arm in arm on a lawn, one wearing a long cranberry knitted scarf, and a freckled sixteen-year-old girl with loose auburn curls in a cranberry cardigan holding a pale plaster mask at her side as she walks toward a glowing purple crystal rock on the roundabout, pink sunrise light, wide shot

good.title: The Leaves Were Empty
good.text: The phones stop ringing at midnight and Crystal Street wakes up on November first with everyone safe. The police find knitting needles in the Kettering leaf pile and nothing else, and the Halloween Safety Committee prints twice as many Babysitter Pledges. You keep one of the needles in your desk drawer. Sometimes, when the phone rings and nobody is there, you wonder what she was trying to tell you.
good.art: A teenager standing at the edge of a scattered pile of autumn leaves on a suburban lawn at dawn, holding a single steel knitting needle, a stack of printed pamphlets on a nearby porch step, a police car pulling away down the street, pale gray morning light, medium wide shot

bittersweet.title: Lights Out by Ten
bittersweet.text: You all make it to November, but the rules win a little. Two friends who held hands on the couch stop sitting together at lunch. Your little neighbor quits babysitting and will not touch a phone after dark. The Shape is quiet now, not gone. Every Halloween you hear needles somewhere down the street, and you leave your porch light on all night, just in case.
bittersweet.art: A teenager sitting on a porch step at night beside a glowing yellow porch light, looking down a quiet leafy street where a faint pale figure in a cranberry cardigan stands far away under a streetlight, a jack-o'-lantern by the door, blue night and yellow light, wide shot

bad.title: A Pleasant Expression
bad.text: On November first your face feels stiff. You smile at breakfast, a small, pleasant, practiced smile, and you cannot stop. You hang up the phone before it rings. You sit on the very edge of the couch, alone. You do not laugh at anything, ever, and your crew watches you knit, row after neat row, a pale blank mask in your lap.
bad.art: A teenager sitting stiffly on the very edge of a plaid couch with a frozen polite smile, knitting a long cranberry strip with steel needles, a pale blank plaster mask resting in their lap, three worried friends in Halloween costumes crowded in the doorway, dim lamp light, medium shot
